Anduril has rolled its first YFQ-44A semi-autonomous fighter jet off the production line at its Arsenal-1 facility in Pickaway County, Ohio — just four months after the manufacturing plant opened in March. The aircraft, a missionized variant of the Fury autonomous fighter built for the U.S. Air Force's Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program, represents a significant milestone in the race to deploy AI-piloted combat vehicles.

The Arsenal-1 facility is designed to produce up to 150 aircraft per year, and the YFQ-44A is being positioned as a key asset for the CCA program, which has initial procurement targets of 100-150 aircraft with long-term goals reaching 1,000 units. Unlike fully autonomous systems, Anduril has emphasized that human operators retain command authority over weapons deployment, adhering to a human-in-the-loop approach for lethal decisions.

The rapid production timeline — from facility opening to first aircraft rollout in just four months — signals a new era in defense manufacturing. The YFQ-44A builds on the Fury platform, which itself was designed from the ground up for autonomous operations, incorporating advanced AI navigation, target identification, and mission planning capabilities.

This development comes amid intense debate over the role of autonomous weapons in modern warfare. While the U.S. military has maintained that humans will always make final decisions on weapons release, the deployment of increasingly capable autonomous platforms is reshaping strategic calculations. The CCA program aims to pair manned aircraft with autonomous wingmen, extending operational capability while reducing risk to human pilots.

Anduril's Ohio facility represents one of the largest investments in domestic defense manufacturing in recent years, reflecting the company's ambition to compete with traditional defense giants like Lockheed Martin and Boeing. The speed of production also highlights how commercial software development practices — rapid iteration, autonomous testing, and agile manufacturing — are being imported into the defense sector.

The first YFQ-44A aircraft is expected to undergo extensive testing before delivery to the Air Force, with operational deployment potentially beginning in 2027. As autonomous aircraft become more prevalent, questions about doctrine, escalation dynamics, and international arms control frameworks will likely intensify.
